Chapter 15, the Yoga of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottamayoga), opens the poem's final stretch of teaching with the celebrated image of an inverted cosmic tree: an eternal aśvattha whose root grows upward and whose branches spread downward, nourished by the three guṇas, its leaves the hymns of the Veda, its lower roots binding human beings to action. Kṛṣṇa urges that this tree of transmigratory existence be felled with the firm weapon of non-attachment, so that the seeker may reach the imperishable state beyond the light of sun, moon and fire from which there is no return — his own supreme abode. He then turns to the individual soul, an eternal fragment of himself that enters a body, draws the senses to itself, and passes from body to body carrying them along as the wind carries scent away from a flower, unseen by the deluded but perceived by those with the eye of knowledge. A further set of verses identifies Kṛṣṇa with the hidden powers that sustain the natural world: the light in the sun, moon and fire; the vigor that upholds the earth and its creatures; the sap-giving Soma that nourishes the plants; the digestive fire in every living body; and the presence seated in the heart of all beings as the source of memory, knowledge, and their loss, at once the object, the author and the knower of the Veda. The chapter reaches its doctrinal climax with the teaching that gives it its name: two Persons exist in the world, the Perishable, which is every finite, changing being, and the unchanging Imperishable; but beyond both stands a third and highest Person, the Supreme Self, who pervades and sustains the three worlds — and this Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa declares, he himself is. Whoever knows him thus, undeluded, as the Supreme Person, becomes a knower of all things and worships him with his whole being. The chapter closes with Kṛṣṇa naming this teaching the most secret of all, and promising that whoever understands it becomes wise and has accomplished everything that life requires.
